intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that annular epidermolytic ichthyosis-1 (AEI1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the keratin-10 gene (KRT10; 148080) on chromosome 17q21.

checks.claim: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis-1 (AEI1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the keratin-10 gene (KRT10).
checks.evidence_quote: Molecular analysis revealed a novel tandem CG to GA 2-bp mutation in the same allele of keratin 10 in affected individuals
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a KRT10 mutation in affected individuals and says inheritance is consistent with autosomal dominant transmission. It never says the mutation is heterozygous, and it does not use the AEI1 designation.

checks.claim: The KRT10 gene is located on chromosome 17q21.
checks.evidence_quote: the rod domain of keratin 10
checks.explanation: The paper names keratin 10. The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene name.

paragraphs.text: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a form of epidermolytic (acanthokeratolytic) ichthyosis. Bullous ichthyosis in infancy or early childhood is followed by persistent hyperkeratotic plaques. Episodes of annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic or scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal extremities come and go. Histology shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (Sahn et al., 1992; Suga et al., 1998).

checks.claim: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a form of epidermolytic (acanthokeratolytic) ichthyosis.
checks.evidence_quote: This kindred may represent a new phenotype of epidermolytic (acanthokeratolytic) ichthyosis.
checks.explanation: Title names annular epidermolytic ichthyosis; abstract frames it as a phenotype of epidermolytic (acanthokeratolytic) ichthyosis.

checks.claim: In annular epidermolytic ichthyosis, bullous ichthyosis in infancy or early childhood is followed by persistent hyperkeratotic plaques.
checks.evidence_quote: developed bullous and ichthyosiform skin lesions at the age of 8 months. Blistering ceased at puberty, but the hyperkeratotic plaques persisted.
checks.explanation: Onset in infancy with blistering, followed by persistent hyperkeratotic plaques.

checks.evidence_quote: Characteristically, they also develop intermittent bouts of annular and polycyclic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal extremities.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes these intermittent episodes directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Histopathologic examination of these annular plaques revealed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis.

(1997) concluded that annular epidermolytic ichthyosis should be considered a variant of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. Suga et al. (1998) likewise described it as a distinct phenotypic variant of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma.

paragraphs.text: Sahn et al. (1992) reported a 30-year-old white woman who developed bullous and ichthyosiform skin lesions at 8 months of age. Blistering stopped at puberty, but the hyperkeratotic plaques persisted. At age 27 years she developed numerous annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and extremities. These plaques itched, enlarged slowly and then resolved. Histopathology showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. On electron microscopy, the annular plaques showed interrupted perinuclear tonofilament rings, which the authors considered consistent with either bullous ichthyotic erythroderma of Brocq or ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens. Two of her 5 children were affected with a bullous type of ichthyosis.

paragraphs.text: Joh et al. (1997) reported the second known occurrence of the disorder, in a family with 2 affected generations. The proband had bullous ichthyosis with bouts of disease activity. During these bouts, numerous annular and polycyclic erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques developed on the trunk and proximal extremities. Histology showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, with abnormal keratin filament networks and clumping of perinuclear tonofilaments.

paragraphs.text: Suga et al. (1998) described a third kindred with annular epidermolytic ichthyosis. Bullous ichthyosis in early childhood was followed by hyperkeratotic lichenified plaques in the flexural areas and on the extensor surfaces. Characteristic intermittent bouts of annular and polycyclic erythematous scaly plaques occurred on the trunk and proximal extremities.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) reported an 8-year-old Brazilian girl, born to nonconsanguineous parents, with a diffuse dermatosis that began in the first months of life. On examination she had erythematous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with prominent borders on the mesogastrium, cubital and popliteal fossae, and inguinal and cervical regions. The plaques were migratory and polycyclic. She also had palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and nasal introitus. She had no hair, nail or mucosal abnormalities. A skin biopsy from the extensor forearm showed acanthosis, papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis, with marked epidermolysis in the granular layer. In a review of the literature in English, Portuguese and Spanish published after the first description by Sahn et al. (1992), the authors found 19 cases of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis in 10 publications.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) noted that the main differential diagnosis of annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva (EKVP). EKVP is distinguished by onset in childhood, the absence of epidermal fragility, and histology without epidermolysis. Their patient was first diagnosed with EKVP, but the diagnosis was revised after a biopsy showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis.

paragraphs.text: In their literature review, Mikilita et al. (2020) found that topical treatments produced little response. These included retinoids, corticosteroids, propylene glycol, calcipotriene and keratolytics. Three reports described a good response to systemic retinoids (acitretin, or low-dose isotretinoin).
